summary: TinyIPFIX is derived from IPFIX (RFC 7011) and adapted for sending smart-meter data in constrained networks such as 6LoWPAN. It keeps the flow-export idea but with a more compact format suited to tiny, low-power devices.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a shrunken version of a reporting format, so little battery-powered meters can send their readings without much data.

questions: how to send smart meter data in constrained networks
how to export data from smart meters
subtitle: Flow data export shrunk for tiny battery-powered meters.

tldr.problem: Smart meters running on small, battery-powered devices in constrained wireless networks (like 6LoWPAN) need to report sensor readings, but the standard IPFIX protocol is too big for their tiny packets and tight memory.
tldr.mechanism: TinyIPFIX compresses the IPFIX message format, shrinking headers and using more efficient field encoding. It keeps IPFIX's core idea of separating templates (descriptions) from data records, making it simple to convert back to standard IPFIX at a gateway.
tldr.outcome: Low-power meters can now send their readings in tiny packets without recharging as often, and gateways can translate TinyIPFIX to IPFIX to feed data into standard monitoring systems.

facts.label: Message structure
facts.value: Header, one or more Sets (Templates or Data)

facts.label: Typical memory
facts.value: 8 to 48 KB RAM, 128 to 512 KB flash

today: RFC 8272 is an Informational RFC published in November 2017. It is not an Internet Standard but documents a practical protocol for use in constrained wireless sensor networks. TinyIPFIX is designed to integrate with the IPFIX framework, and gateways can convert it to standard IPFIX for use in larger monitoring systems.

sections.title: The Problem with Constrained Devices
sections.content:
Smart meters that monitor electric usage, water consumption, or temperature in homes and buildings are often low-cost, low-power devices with limited memory and processing power. When grouped into wireless networks using 6LoWPAN (IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks), these meters face hard constraints: 128 KB of program memory might be typical, 8 to 10 KB of RAM, and a radio transceiver that must be powered off to save battery. IEEE 802.15.4, the radio standard used, limits each packet to 102 octets of usable payload after headers.

The standard IPFIX protocol (RFC 7011), designed for flow monitoring on general networks, produces messages that are too verbose for such devices. TinyIPFIX solves this by compressing the format while keeping IPFIX's structure so that conversion back to standard IPFIX is straightforward.
sections.plainLanguage: Smart meters are tiny, cheap devices that run on batteries and can only send very small radio messages. IPFIX is a standard reporting format, but it is too big and complicated for them to use, so TinyIPFIX shrinks it down.

sections.title: Architecture and Components
sections.content:
TinyIPFIX follows the same role structure as IPFIX: an Exporter is a device (like a smart meter) that sends data, a Collector receives it, and an Exporting Process or Collecting Process is the software doing the work. A TinyIPFIX Proxy or Concentrator is an intermediate device that can receive TinyIPFIX messages from multiple meters, combine or process them, and forward them either as TinyIPFIX or converted to standard IPFIX. Because TinyIPFIX removes a 16-byte message export timestamp that IPFIX requires, record-level timestamps in the data fields themselves can provide the timing information applications need.

Messages flow one way: from exporters to collectors over UDP (occasionally TCP or SCTP). The devices do not need to receive messages, so they can keep their radios off most of the time, saving power.
sections.plainLanguage: Meters send data to a collector using TinyIPFIX. A proxy or concentrator can be placed between them to gather data from many meters and send it elsewhere. Everything goes one way, so meters never have to listen.

sections.title: Hardware and Network Constraints
sections.content:
TinyIPFIX is designed around four hard constraints. Hardware: devices have 8 to 48 KB of RAM, 128 to 512 KB of flash, and must run protocols in tight memory. Energy: battery-powered devices might run for years on two AA batteries if they power down their radio when not transmitting. Packet size: IEEE 802.15.4 radio packets are only 102 octets, and fragmentation (splitting large messages across packets) is dangerous because losing any one fragment loses the entire message. Transport: unlike IPFIX's default requirement for SCTP, TinyIPFIX uses UDP because 6LoWPAN includes header compression for UDP but not TCP or SCTP, leaving more space for sensor data.

The RFC addresses all four by compressing the message header, removing unnecessary fields, and recommending UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices are tiny, batteries are precious, messages are small, and compression is essential. TinyIPFIX is built to fit all of this.

sections.title: Message Format and Compression
sections.content:
TinyIPFIX messages consist of a compact header, followed by one or more Sets. A Set is either a Template Set (describing what fields will appear in data) or a Data Set (containing actual meter readings). The header is much smaller than IPFIX's: TinyIPFIX removes the export timestamp, uses shorter fields for message length, and omits some optional information. Each field in a Template Record includes its Information Element number (what it is, like temperature or power usage) and its length in octets. Data Records simply list field values in the order specified by a template.

Because meters typically have the same sensors and same data layout every time, templates rarely change. The RFC recommends periodically re-sending templates even over UDP so that if a template message is lost, collectors can still decode later data by re-requesting or waiting for the next template transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: A TinyIPFIX message says 'here are the fields I have' (the template), then 'here are today's readings' (the data). Keeping templates small and templates consistent makes everything fit in tiny packets.

sections.title: Converting to Standard IPFIX
sections.content: At a gateway or concentrator, TinyIPFIX messages can be converted (mediated) to standard IPFIX for feeding into existing monitoring and analysis systems. The process is simple: expand the TinyIPFIX message header to IPFIX's larger format, add the missing export timestamp, expand the Set headers, and expand Template Record headers to their IPFIX form. No data is lost or reordered, so the conversion is lossless. This means that even though smart meters use TinyIPFIX internally, their data can seamlessly integrate into IPFIX-based data collection infrastructure already in place at many organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway can take a TinyIPFIX message and expand it back into a full IPFIX message that standard software can understand.

sections.title: When to Use TinyIPFIX
sections.content: TinyIPFIX is designed for long-term measurement applications where real-time updates are not critical. Ideal uses include monitoring building temperature every 5 minutes, measuring water or electricity usage hourly, or tracking structural health of bridges with occasional sensor readings. The protocol is not suitable for applications where packet loss is intolerable (such as detecting intrusions or triggering emergency responses) because it uses unreliable UDP with no acknowledgments. It is also not suitable for applications that require a timestamp on every message export event, since it does not include that field. However, for accounting-style applications where data is stored for billing or offline analysis, TinyIPFIX is an excellent fit. The RFC cites real-world deployments such as environmental monitoring in a 70-meter redwood tree (5-minute intervals) and habitat monitoring for animals using wireless sensor networks.
sections.plainLanguage: TinyIPFIX works great for meters that check in every few minutes and want to save battery. Do not use it for emergencies or when you cannot afford to lose a single message.
